analysis.one_liner: Ends Energy Department review of natural gas exports and requires approval of LNG export terminals.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 217–188 on November 20, 2025 — 206 of 219 voting Republicans for, 11 of 214 voting Democrats for — and it now sits on the Senate calendar with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill repeals the requirement that the Department of Energy approve natural gas exports and imports, and gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) exclusive authority over export and import terminals — with a mandate to treat any export or import as automatically in the public interest. That removes the current step where the government weighs exports against domestic supply needs before approving them. The House passed it mostly along party lines in November 2025, and it is now waiting on the Senate calendar.
analysis.who_benefits: LNG export companies and natural gas producers gain the most: they would no longer need Energy Department authorization to export, and FERC would be required to deem any export or import terminal application consistent with the public interest, making near-automatic approval the rule [S2][S3]. A presidential carve-out is preserved so exports to sanctioned countries or state sponsors of terrorism can still be blocked [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: LNG exporters and natural gas producers

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the sections of the Natural Gas Act requiring Department of Energy approval of natural gas exports and imports, including the free-trade-agreement determinations that currently gate exports to countries without a US trade deal.

Gives FERC exclusive authority over siting, construction, expansion, and operation of export and import facilities, and requires FERC to deem the export or import of natural gas consistent with the public interest — meaning the regulator cannot weigh domestic needs against exports when deciding.
Preserves the President's authority under existing sanctions laws to prohibit exports or imports to sanctioned countries, countries designated state sponsors of terrorism, and sanctioned persons.

analysis.who_pays: Households, manufacturers, and utilities that buy natural gas would bear the risk: once exports are deemed automatically in the public interest, gas can be shipped abroad without anyone weighing what that does to domestic prices or supply. The public also loses the current Energy Department public-interest review, and FERC's discretion to deny a terminal is removed [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Natural gas consumers; the DOE export review

drawbacks.text: Removing DOE's approval requirement eliminates the current process in which exports are evaluated against domestic supply needs before being authorized — under the bill, FERC must treat any export as consistent with the public interest and cannot deny one on those grounds.

Consolidating all authority in FERC with a mandated public-interest finding strips the regulator of discretion: it could not reject a terminal application on public-interest grounds even if exports raised domestic gas prices for households and manufacturers.

The national-security backstop is narrower than current review: it relies on the President's existing sanctions authorities and a 'state sponsor of terrorism' designation, leaving exports to other countries — including non-allied ones without sanctions — unchecked by any public-interest test.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Exporters get speed and certainty, and the sanctions carve-out answers part of the security objection. But the trade is one-sided: the bill doesn't merely speed up review, it deletes the domestic public-interest test entirely and instructs FERC to find every export in the public interest. An honest supporter would concede that this shifts the risk of higher domestic gas prices onto consumers and manufacturers, with no process left to weigh or mitigate it.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it mostly along party lines in November 2025, and it is now sitting on the Senate calendar with no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 6, 2025, and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee; a subcommittee forwarded it on a 15–13 vote and the full committee ordered it reported 26–23 on June 25.
The committee reported it on September 11, 2025 (H. Rept. 119-269), placing it on the Union Calendar.

On November 17 the Rules Committee reported H. Res. 879, a closed rule — meaning no amendments from the floor were allowed — bundling H.R. 1949 with six other energy-related measures for one hour of debate each and one motion to recommit.
The House passed the bill on November 20, 2025, 217–188 (Roll no. 304): 206 of 219 voting Republicans for, 0 against; 11 of 214 voting Democrats for, 188 against.
The Senate received the bill December 2, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 286) on December 8, 2025, where it awaits further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, LNG export companies and natural gas producers: House passage moves their goal of an unrestricted export regime forward without DOE review. If the Senate never takes it up, natural gas consumers and the Energy Department's public-interest authority are better off than they would have been under the law.

industries.industry: LNG export terminal developers and exporters
industries.note: The bill deletes the DOE export-authorization step and requires FERC to deem every export in the public interest, so terminals that today can be denied on domestic-need grounds become near-automatic approvals. The industry's gain comes directly from removing the check that weighs its exports against domestic supply and prices.

Producers gain a larger, less restricted export market for their gas, which supports higher prices at the wellhead. The same dynamic tends to raise what households and manufacturers pay domestically as more gas is committed to export.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and utilities that buy natural gas
industries.note: Large industrial gas users and gas-fired utilities currently benefit from DOE's authority to weigh domestic demand against export demand. The bill removes that counterweight, leaving them exposed to whatever price effects expanded exports produce.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, which is where most House-passed bills wait indefinitely — getting floor time requires the majority leader to schedule it. With only 11 House Democrats supporting the bill, it would likely need 60 votes in the Senate to overcome a filibuster, so the realistic path is that it stalls this Congress unless it is attached to a larger must-pass package.
